findings.headline: MTFP forecasts £2.842m funding gap in 2027/28, rising to £3.360m in 2028/29
findings.detail: The council is explicitly allocating the 2025/26 underspend to manage upcoming structural funding gaps rather than to one-off commitments. Of the £1.261m underspend, £611k is being transferred to the Budget Risk Reserve specifically "hypothecated for future one-off use to mitigate the gap already reported in the 2027/28 Medium-Term Financial Plan" at £2.842m, increasing to £3.360m in 2028/29.
findings.matters: The council faces significant structural funding gaps ahead that it plans to cover with reserve draws rather than sustainable savings. The underspend is being treated as a tool to manage MTFP gaps, not strengthen the balance sheet.
findings.figures: 2027/28 gap £2.842m, 2028/29 gap £3.360m, £611k underspend earmarked to mitigate
findings.quote: It is recommended that the remaining outturn variance is transferred to the Council's Budget Risk Reserve and hypothecated for future one-off use to mitigate the gap already reported in the 2027/28 Medium-Term Financial Plan. These were £2.842m in 2027/28, increasing to £3.360m in 2028/29.

findings.headline: £572k of housing repairs shifted from capital to revenue, indicating capital maintenance underfunding
findings.detail: HRA repairs and maintenance overspent by £995k. The report attributes this to higher levels of expenditure being charged to revenue (£572k) alongside lower capital works delivered by Housing Property Services. This represents a structural shift of maintenance costs from capital (borrowable/funded) to revenue (funded from rents).
findings.matters: Shifting maintenance from capital to revenue increases annual cost pressures on rents and indicates the HRA may be underfunding capital maintenance, with reactive maintenance bleeding into revenue.
findings.figures: £572k shifted to revenue, £995k total repairs and maintenance overspend
findings.quote: The overspend reflects higher levels of repair and maintenance expenditure charged to revenue (£572k), together with a lower level of capital works delivered by Housing Property Services. This has resulted in a greater proportion of costs being charged to revenue, increasing pressure on the repairs and maintenance budget.

findings.headline: HRA working balance at £3.117m is below the prudent minimum of £3.7m with ongoing void rate stress
findings.detail: The HRA working balance at year-end stands at £3.117m against a minimum prudent balance of £3.7m. Actual void rate was 4.54% against forecast of 3.83%, creating ongoing rent loss pressure. The business plan assumes a void rate of 2%, creating a significant gap between actual and target.
findings.matters: Housing finance is operating with reserves below the prudent minimum, and actual rental income is under pressure from void rates significantly above the long-term business plan assumption. This constrains HRA financial flexibility.
findings.figures: HRA balance £3.117m vs minimum £3.7m, void rate 4.54% actual vs 3.83% forecast vs 2.0% plan
findings.quote: The HRA balance for 2025/26 is below the minimum balance... The revised estimate assumed void rate at 3.83% - actual void rate 4.54%, resulting in further rent loss.

findings.headline: Enterprise Zone business rates reserve depleted from £5.5m to £1.5m in single year
findings.detail: The Enterprise Zone business rates reserve fell from £5.542m (1 April 2025) to £1.468m (31 March 2026), a reduction of £4.074m in a single financial year. The council states this was primarily used to invest in Stephenson Memorial Hall capital costs and support economic development activities.
findings.matters: A material ringfenced reserve has been substantially depleted, reducing future financial flexibility for economic development activities and capital investment. The reserve now provides limited buffer.
findings.figures: Opening £5.542m, closing £1.468m, reduction £4.074m (73% depletion)
findings.quote: The total balance on these earmarked reserves decreased by £3.8m during the year, mainly due to the use of Markham Vale retained business rates growth to invest in Stephenson Memorial Hall capital costs and continued support for various economic development activities.

findings.headline: Revitalising the Heart of Chesterfield delayed by unforeseen archaeological findings
findings.detail: The £4.906m LUF-funded regeneration scheme experienced programme slippage of £1.171m. Practical completion was achieved in June 2026 for Market Square and New Square, but archaeological findings at Rykneld Square have delayed that element, which is now being redesigned.
findings.matters: Unforeseen archaeological discoveries have delayed a major town centre regeneration scheme and triggered redesign work, extending delivery timescales for a scheme already subject to contractor extension requests.
findings.figures: £4.906m budget, £1.171m slippage, archaeological findings requiring redesign at Rykneld Square
findings.quote: Due to archaeological findings, works in Rykneld Square have been delayed, and are currently being redesigned.

findings.headline: Stephenson Memorial Hall delayed beyond April 2026 target due to structural defects
findings.detail: The £9.840m LUF-funded Stephenson Memorial Hall capital scheme encountered significant delays caused by structural issues discovered during construction. A commercial settlement was agreed with the contractor and an Extension of Time granted, pushing practical completion from April 2026 to June 2026 (subsequently "Summer 2026"). The scheme shows £1.199m slippage against revised budget.
findings.matters: A major capital investment faced material delays due to structural defects, indicating either that initial surveys were inadequate or that latent issues emerged during delivery. This has extended project duration and cost profile.
findings.figures: £9.840m budget, £1.199m slippage, originally April 2026 completion now June/Summer 2026
findings.quote: Work has been progressing reasonably well although there have been some significant delays, caused mainly by structural issues. It was initially expected that work would be completed by April 2026. A commercial settlement was agreed with the contractors, and an Extension of Time was granted to June 2026.

findings.headline: Legal Services spent £437k on interim appointments to maintain service delivery
findings.detail: Legal Services within the Chief Executives directorate recorded a £437k overspend attributed entirely to using interim appointments to maintain service delivery while permanent recruitment was underway. This suggests the council has not been able to fill these posts permanently and is sustaining the function through temporary staffing.
findings.matters: Legal Services is a core corporate function; inability to recruit permanently and dependence on expensive interim cover indicates a structural staffing problem and concentration of cost risk.
findings.figures: £437k overspend on interim Legal Services appointments in 2025/26
findings.quote: This is made up of £437k overspend within Legal Services, largely due to the use of interim appointments to maintain service delivery while permanent recruitment has been underway

findings.headline: Finance service reports persistent difficulty recruiting to senior and specialist posts
findings.detail: The Finance directorate recorded a £104k underspend in 2025/26 driven by a high level of vacancies in senior and specialist finance roles. The report states the service "has experienced ongoing challenges in securing suitably qualified and experienced candidates" despite sustained recruitment activity, leaving key posts vacant and necessitating temporary and agency resource to fill the gap.
findings.matters: The Finance function itself cannot recruit permanent staff to critical posts. This creates dependency on temporary resources for core financial control and raises questions about the council's permanent capacity in financial management and the continuity of financial oversight.
findings.figures: Multiple senior and specialist vacancies in Finance offset by increased temp and agency costs
findings.quote: Despite sustained recruitment activity, the service has experienced ongoing challenges in securing suitably qualified and experienced candidates. As a result, a number of key posts have remained vacant generating in-year savings on employee costs.

findings.headline: Careline service closed from 1 August 2026 after failing to reach operational breakeven
findings.detail: The Careline service was modelled to breakeven at 1,600 customers at £14.50 per week, generating £1.2m annual income. Customer numbers remained consistently below this throughout 2025/26, requiring a £339k reserve draw to cover the in-year shortfall. Following public consultation, the council formally decided on 19 May 2026 to close the service, marking the end of what was intended as a self-financing operation.
findings.matters: A revenue-raising service designed to be self-sustaining failed to achieve market demand, forcing the council to discontinue it and manage the transition costs. This signals that demand assumptions for new income-generating schemes carry execution risk.
findings.figures: 1,600 breakeven customers, £14.50/week price point, £1.2m income target, £339k reserve draw to cover shortfall
findings.quote: The Careline business model assumed a breakeven point of 1,600 customers at a price point of £14.50 per week and an income target of £1.2m. Customer numbers remained below the level required to achieve a break-even position during 2025/26, resulting in a year-end pressure on the service.

findings.paper_title: Period 2 2026-27 Forecast Monitoring Cabinet Report FINAL
findings.headline: National pay award offer of 3.3% creates unresolved £25k cost exposure against 3% budget assumption
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget assumed a 3% NJC pay award. The National Employers offered 3.3% consolidated from 1 April 2026, but this offer remains ungreed. A 0.3% increase would add approximately £25k pa to cost pressures.
findings.matters: Unresolved cost exposure in a material budget line; outcome depends on ongoing pay negotiations and could materialise quickly
findings.figures: c£25k additional cost pressure from 0.3% pay award increase
findings.quote: A 0.3% increase in pay could add a further c£25k pa to the cost pressures for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Period 2 2026-27 Forecast Monitoring Cabinet Report FINAL
findings.headline: Stephenson Memorial Hall venue refurbishment creating £200k year one operational cost pressure
findings.detail: The refurbished Stephenson Memorial Hall venue has a £200k year one operational pressure in the MTFP that is expected to be fully utilised. The council is still refining detailed operational and maintenance requirements, suggesting scope may not be fully defined.
findings.matters: New significant operational cost from capital project coming online; ongoing refinement indicates potential for further cost escalation
findings.figures: £200k pressure expected to be fully utilised
findings.quote: the potential delivery cost of year one operations for the Stephenson Memorial Hall venue has been reflected in the Period 2 forecast based on draft figures. The £200k pressure approved in the MTFP for these purposes is expected to be fully utilised.

findings.paper_title: Period 2 2026-27 Forecast Monitoring Cabinet Report FINAL
findings.headline: Careline service closure will cost £561k in 2026/27, requiring drawdown from reserves
findings.detail: The closure of the Careline service creates both one-off and in-year financial pressures estimated at £561k. The council will fund this through the Careline reserve (up to £400k), flexible use of capital receipts (up to £400k), and the General Fund Budget Risk Reserve if required.
findings.matters: Shows the council drawing down reserves to manage a service closure decision; indicates pressure on reserve buffers that lenders track
findings.figures: £561k total impact; up to £400k from Careline reserve, up to £400k from capital receipts flexibility, remainder from Budget Risk Reserve
findings.quote: The closure of the Careline service gives rise to both one-off and in-year financial pressures in 2026/27, currently estimated at £561k.

findings.headline: Internal audit found 'Limited assurance' on housing voids control
findings.detail: The internal audit review of the council's management of vacant housing properties resulted in a Limited assurance opinion, indicating control weaknesses. This is a specific audit finding that differs from the overall reasonable assurance opinion.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on void management in an HRA already facing pressure on working balance suggests control weaknesses in a high-impact area affecting costs and income.
findings.figures: 1 limited assurance report out of 23 internal audit reports issued in 2025/26
findings.quote: The internal audit review of housing voids resulted in a Limited assurance opinion.

findings.headline: Ongoing recruitment difficulties in specialist finance and audit roles
findings.detail: The council continues to experience difficulties recruiting suitably qualified staff in Finance, Internal Audit, Legal, and technical services roles. The statement notes remuneration is not sufficiently competitive within the wider labour market and recruitment challenges create ongoing risks to service resilience and organisational capacity.
findings.matters: Inability to recruit and retain experienced finance and audit staff weakens the council's internal control environment and financial management capability, creating governance and operational risks.
findings.figures: Turnover rate 7.99% excluding casual employees
findings.quote: The Council continues to experience challenges in recruiting and retaining suitably qualified and experienced employees in a number of specialist and technical roles, particularly where remuneration is not sufficiently competitive within the wider labour market and market supplements are not available.

findings.headline: National redistribution of resources has left Chesterfield with 'sizeable financial challenge for future years'
findings.detail: Despite the introduction of a multi-year government settlement in December 2025 that provides clarity on funding, the council states that resource redistribution has created significant structural funding gaps ahead. The council acknowledges it must develop 'robust ongoing budget proposals' for future years.
findings.matters: An acknowledged 'sizeable' funding gap with structural drivers (not temporary) indicates the council faces material budget pressures that cannot be resolved through small efficiencies alone.
findings.figures: Unspecified 'sizeable financial challenge for future years'
findings.quote: Whilst the introduction of a confirmed multi-year government settlement provides clarity regarding future funding levels and assists medium term planning, the national redistribution of resources has left Chesterfield with a sizeable financial challenge for future years.

findings.headline: 2025/26 budget balanced largely with one-off savings and managed underspends
findings.detail: The council balanced its 2025/26 budget using £730k from a deliberately managed underspend in 2024/25, £903k from better-than-expected outcomes in prior-year proposals, and £676k in one-off grant funding. This reliance on one-off items and timing suggests structural budget pressures not yet fully resolved.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on non-recurring savings to balance annual budgets is a warning sign that the council has not yet identified enough permanent cost reductions or income growth to close structural funding gaps.
findings.figures: £730k one-off use of managed 2024/25 underspend; £903k ongoing savings from prior-year proposals; £676k available grant funding; £150k additional income from fees and charges
findings.quote: This budget was constructed in accordance with the Council's budget principles and balanced with £903k ongoing savings from better-than-expected outcomes from budget proposals delivered in previous financial years, £150k additional income from revised fees and charges, the application of £676k available grant funding for particular services and the one-off use of £730k from a deliberately managed 2024/25 underspend.

findings.headline: External auditor will disclaim opinion on 2025/26 financial statements
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars LLP will not provide an unqualified opinion on the 2025/26 accounts. The external auditor is rebuilding assurance on a multi-year schedule due to national backlogs, and backstop arrangements mean they will disclaim their opinion rather than provide full audit assurance.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means no independent verification that the council's financial statements are accurate or complete, reducing audit assurance and increasing reliance on internal controls.
findings.figures: Disclaimer of opinion for 2025/26; backstop dates extend to 2027/28
findings.quote: As a result of the backstop arrangements, Forvis Mazars are in the process of rebuilding assurance which will take a number of years thereby resulting in a disclaimer of opinion on the Council's financial statements for 2025/26.

findings.headline: HRA working balance projected to fall below minimum due to cost pressures
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account (HRA) is experiencing ongoing financial pressures from rising maintenance costs, voids, and disrepair claims. The latest MTFP projections show the working balance will temporarily dip below the minimum acceptable level before recovering in subsequent years through increased rental income and reduced staff costs.
findings.matters: HRA liquidity stress indicates reduced financial flexibility to handle unexpected housing costs or compliance failures, and challenges the council's ability to maintain housing stock maintenance standards.
findings.figures: Working balance projected to temporarily fall below minimum; £61m loss over 30-year business plan period from government rent policy imposing rent caps; £1.5m annual income loss from rent cap policy
findings.quote: As a result of ongoing financial pressures, particularly in relation to rising maintenance costs, voids, disrepair claims, and capital investment plans, the latest MTPF shows this working balance is projected to temporarily fall below the minimum working balance.

findings.headline: £500k contingency fund established for 2026/27 to manage acknowledged 'inherent risk of further cost variances, schedule delays, and unforeseen challenges' on major schemes
findings.detail: The council is establishing a £500k Capital Programme Contingency Fund for 2026/27 (funded from Markham Vale Business Rates Reserve) with delegated Cabinet authority to approve drawdowns. This is explicitly to manage risks on high-value schemes reaching completion, recognizing the scale, complexity, and inflationary pressures on current projects.
findings.matters: A substantial contingency signals the council recognizes material cost and schedule risks on major projects. This uses reserves that could otherwise support discretionary investment or maintain financial resilience. It also indicates projects may not deliver on time or within budget.
findings.figures: £500k contingency fund for 2026/27
findings.quote: Given their scale and complexity, there is an inherent risk of further cost variances, schedule delays, and unforeseen challenges as schemes reach completion.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecasts described as 'continually changing'; council reallocating £300k of Stephenson Hall funding from receipts to reserves to 'reduce reliance on capital receipts'
findings.detail: The programme depends on £8.7m capital receipts from asset disposals, which the council notes are 'continually changing as delays are encountered in relation to some disposals'. In response, the council is shifting £300k of Stephenson Hall project funding from capital receipts to the Markham Vale Business Rates Reserve, explicitly stated as intended to reduce reliance on receipts.
findings.matters: Unreliable capital receipt forecasts indicate asset disposal plans may be at risk or delayed. The reallocation signals the council has concerns about realizing expected receipts. For lenders, this reduces financial flexibility and raises questions about the council's ability to fund projects as planned or generate cashflow from asset sales.
findings.figures: £8.734m capital receipts assumed in programme; £300k reallocation for Stephenson Hall
findings.quote: Capital receipts forecasts are continually changing as delays are encountered in relation to some disposals whilst opportunities arise to accelerate others.

findings.headline: Multiple major schemes experiencing specific delivery delays: Hollis Lane awaiting planning, Rykneld Square delayed for archaeology, Stephenson Hall heritage complexity, Staveley 21 infrastructure delays
findings.detail: Four key capital projects all face documented delays: Hollis Lane Link Road awaiting planning with works now expected end 2026/27; Rykneld Square delayed for archaeological investigation (delivery Summer 2026); Stephenson Memorial Hall facing heritage-related construction complexity (Summer 2026 completion); Staveley 21 waiting on electrical infrastructure connection for practical completion.
findings.matters: These are major regeneration and town deal schemes (significant grant-funded). Multiple concurrent delays on complex projects indicate execution risk, particularly in an inflationary environment where delays increase costs. This signals project management challenges across the portfolio.
findings.figures: Multiple delays ranging 3-6+ months from original timescales
findings.quote: Progress in Rykneld Square has been delayed due to the need for further archaeological investigations. It is likely that Rykneld Square will be delivered in Summer 2026.

findings.headline: Slippage of £3.9m from 2025/26 indicates execution delays on major capital schemes
findings.detail: Major schemes scheduled for completion in 2025/26 have been delayed into 2026/27. This represents a significant slippage in delivery timescales, reflecting challenges in project sequencing and execution on the council's key regeneration and investment programmes.
findings.matters: Slippage indicates execution challenges on major projects and affects the council's ability to generate expected capital receipts from asset completions. For lenders, delays suggest either planning shortcomings or project management risks that could affect cash flow and financial resilience.
findings.quote: Slippage of £3.903m from the 2025/26 Capital Programme into 2026/27 has been identified in relation to major capital schemes scheduled for completion in 2025/26.

findings.headline: New borrowing at 5.1% versus existing portfolio average of 3.6% increases incremental debt service costs by 150 basis points
findings.detail: The council's current borrowing portfolio averages 3.6% interest (£122.2m at that rate). Treasury assumptions project new long-term borrowing at 5.1%, reflecting current gilt yields and PWLB pricing. The HRA currently pays £4.7m annual interest on average debt of £128.9m. New HRA borrowing will cost significantly more per pound borrowed.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs on incremental debt reduce the council's financial flexibility and lock in higher debt service costs over decades. Combined with depleting reserves, this materially changes the council's cash position and limits capacity to invest in services or respond to new pressures.
findings.figures: Existing portfolio average rate 3.6%; new borrowing forecast at 5.1%; HRA interest budget £4.7m on average debt £128.9m (rate 3.6%)
findings.quote: For the purpose of setting the budget, it has been assumed that new treasury investments will be made at an average rate/yield of 3.3%, and that new long-term loans will be borrowed at an average rate of 5.1%.

findings.headline: Liability benchmark forecasts structural external borrowing requirement rising from £123.7m to £153.8m (24% increase) by 2028-29
findings.detail: The council's liability benchmark—the minimum external borrowing needed to fund current capital and revenue plans at minimum £10m investment level—increases £30.1m over the forecast period. This indicates the council will transition to a structural long-term borrower position with rising cumulative borrowing needs.
findings.matters: A 24% increase in the estimated borrowing requirement over three years signals growing financial pressure and tightening fiscal position. For lenders assessing creditworthiness, this indicates diminishing debt capacity and reduced headroom for new commitments.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark: £123.7m (31.3.25 actual) rising to £153.8m (31.3.29 forecast)—increases of £7.8m, £16.0m, £4.9m, and £1.4m in successive years
findings.quote: The table above demonstrates that the Council expects to be a long-term borrower in the future.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme triggers new external borrowing requirement from 2026-27 onwards
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account Capital Financing Requirement increases from 2026-27 due to an HRA capital programme. Whilst General Fund CFR reduces after 2025-26, the combined total CFR rises from £190.4m to £209.0m by 2028-29, forcing new external borrowing. The council expects to borrow in 2026-27 to fund the capital programme.
findings.matters: Housing capital investment increases the council's borrowing need and annual debt service costs. At the forecasted borrowing rate of 5.1%, each £10m borrowed adds approximately £0.51m annual interest cost. This commits future revenue to debt repayment.
findings.figures: HRA CFR increases from 2026-27; total CFR rising from £190.4m to £209.0m by 2028-29; new borrowing forecast at 5.1% average rate
findings.quote: The HRA CFR increases from 2026/27 financial year due to the HRA capital programme.

findings.headline: Council's useable reserves forecast to fall £10.7m by 2028-29 while capital is financed from internal resources rather than external borrowing
findings.detail: The council is deploying internal borrowing—using available balance sheet resources to fund capital rather than borrowing externally. By 2028-29, balance sheet resources fall from £75.9m to £65.2m while internal borrowing (reserve drawdown) rises from £58.4m to £96.5m. Treasury investments are forecast to move from a £17.5m surplus to a £31.3m deficit by 2028-29.
findings.matters: A council eating into reserves to fund capital is a sign of financial constraint. It signals reduced capacity to absorb unexpected revenue falls or spending overruns, and reduced liquid resources available for operational needs. Lenders use reserve levels as a key indicator of financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources £75.9m (actual 31.3.25) declining to £65.2m (forecast 31.3.29); internal borrowing rising from £58.4m to £96.5m; treasury investments from +£17.5m to -£31.3m
findings.quote: Investments are forecast to fall as useable reserves are utilised to finance the HRA and General Fund capital programmes, however a minimum of £10 million investments will be maintained in order to retain Professional Client status under MiFID 2.

findings.headline: Near-term treasury investments eliminated; £10.0m held indefinitely for professional provider status
findings.detail: Council's near-term liquid investments forecast to drop from £7.4m to £0.0m. Offsetting this, £10.0m in longer-term investments must be held indefinitely to maintain professional status with finance service providers, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: The elimination of near-term liquid reserves combined with a mandatory long-term holding constrains the council's ability to manage short-term cash fluctuations or respond to unexpected expenses.
findings.figures: Near-term investments: £7.4m (31.3.2025) → £0.0m (31.3.2027). Required permanent holding: £10.0m
findings.quote: £10.0m of the above investments is shown as a longer-term investment as this £10.0m is required to be held indefinitely by the Council is order for it to maintain a professional status with finance service providers.

findings.headline: £36.9m investment property portfolio must generate 5.9% net return to support revenue budget sustainability
findings.detail: The council holds £36.9m in investment property (31 March 2025) and is dependent on this generating a 5.9% net return after costs. This material reliance on property investment returns creates exposure to market downturns, rental income volatility, and valuation risk.
findings.matters: A significant portion of revenue budget sustainability depends on maintaining investment property yields; any downturn in property valuations or rental income could directly impact the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Investment property: £36.9m. Expected net return: 5.9%
findings.quote: The Authority also holds investment property worth £36.9m as of 31st March 2025. These investments are expected to provide a net return after all costs of 5.9%.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing to £209.0m by 2029, with HRA component increasing £9.2m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Total CFR grows from £191.7m (31.3.2026) to £202.0m (31.3.2027) to £209.0m (31.3.2029). The HRA component is growing rapidly—£9.2m increase in 2026/27 alone—and is forecast to reach £152.8m by 2029. This represents long-term debt obligations that will constrain future revenue budgets.
findings.matters: A growing CFR signals increasing long-term debt obligations and revenue servicing requirements that will constrain the council's budget flexibility for decades, affecting debt capacity and creditworthiness.
findings.quote: The General Fund CFR is expected to increase by £1.1m during 2026/27 and the HRA CFR is expected to increase by £9.2m during the same period.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising from 8.4% to 10.9% of net revenue stream by 2027/28
findings.detail: As interest and MRP charges grow, the proportion of revenue budget consumed by financing costs increases. The General Fund proportion of net revenue stream rises from 8.4% in 2024/25 to 10.2% in 2026/27 and 10.9% in 2027/28. This leaves less revenue available for service delivery.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs as a percentage of revenue budget indicates worsening debt serviceability and reduced financial flexibility to respond to pressures or invest in services.
findings.figures: Financing costs General Fund: 8.4% (2024/25) → 10.2% (2026/27) → 10.9% (2027/28) of net revenue stream
findings.quote: Although capital expenditure is not charged directly to the revenue budget, interest payable on loans and MRP are charged to revenue. The charge is known as financing costs; this is compared to the net revenue stream

findings.headline: Debt financing rises fivefold to £12.5m as primary capital funding source, despite lower overall capital spend
findings.detail: Debt financing jumps from £2.6m in 2025/26 to £12.5m in 2026/27—a 381% increase. This occurs despite total capital expenditure remaining similar (£59.5m to £44.0m). As of 31 December 2025, the council held £122.2m of borrowing at an average interest rate of 3.6%.
findings.matters: A sharp increase in borrowing to fund capital that is actually declining raises questions about cash position, financial sustainability, and the growing burden of debt servicing on future revenue budgets.
findings.figures: Debt financing 2025/26: £2.6m; 2026/27: £12.5m. Outstanding borrowing: £122.2m at 3.6% average rate
findings.quote: Debt is only a temporary source of finance, since loans and leases must be repaid, and this is therefore replaced over time by other financing, usually from revenue which is known as minimum revenue provision (MRP).

findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure collapses from £35.9m to £10.0m in 2026/27, with zero planned for 2028/29
findings.detail: After forecasting £35.9m of General Fund capital spend in 2025/26, the council has planned just £10.0m for 2026/27 and explicitly states no capital plans for 2028/29. This 72% contraction signals either project delays, completion of a major programme, or constrained finances. Main 2026/27 projects are Stephenson Memorial Hall (£9.8m), Staveley Town Deal (£9.3m), and Revitalising Heart of Chesterfield (£4.9m).
findings.matters: A sudden collapse in capital plans could indicate financial distress, delayed or cancelled projects, or a shift in priorities that affects long-term service delivery and council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: General Fund capital: £35.9m (2025/26 forecast) → £10.0m (2026/27 budget) → £0.0m (2028/29 budget)
findings.quote: Capital plans for the general fund do not cover the 2028/29 year, therefore no capital expenditure is so far assumed for this year.

findings.headline: Council reserves at risk threshold: CFO warns further material use would leave council unable to manage risks
findings.detail: The council is now drawing on multiple reserves to balance budgets: £273k from Budget Risk reserve in 2026/27, plus ongoing £267k annual draw on Markham Vale Enterprise Zone reserve for economic development, plus £130k from reserves to fund time-limited pressures. The CFO explicitly warns that reserves are "now at a level whereby any significant further use would leave the Council exposed to risk and unable to manage potential risks."
findings.matters: The council is approaching reserve depletion with unresolved gaps ahead. The CFO's warning language indicates material financial stress and limited buffer for unexpected costs or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: Budget Risk reserve use 2026/27 £273k; ongoing Markham Vale draw £267k per annum; total reserve draw 2026/27 £670k; projected Budget Risk balance 31 March 2026 £2.205m, projected use to £1.757m
findings.quote: Whilst the use of reserves to date has been deemed to be affordable, they are now at a level whereby any significant further use would leave the Council exposed to risk and unable to manage potential risks.

findings.headline: Pay award costs already overrunning: 2025/26 award was higher than budgeted, requiring £300k adjustment
findings.detail: The 2025/26 pay award came in at 3.2% (vs the amount originally assumed in the MTFP), requiring a retrospective £300k addition to 2026/27 budgets just to cover the cost of that higher award. The 2026/27 MTFP assumes a further c3% pay increase. The CFO notes pay negotiations outcomes are uncertain and may require revisiting.
findings.matters: Pay costs are a variable that the council cannot fully control, and recent history shows estimates can miss by material amounts. With recruitment already difficult, the council has limited flexibility to resist pay pressure.
findings.figures: 2025/26 pay award 3.2% vs budgeted; £300k adjustment required into 2026/27; assumed 2026/27 pay award c3%; assumed future pay award 2%
findings.quote: In July the National Employers agreed a 3.2% local government pay award for 2025/26. This was higher than assumed in the previous MTFP and as a consequence £300k has been added into 2026/27 to compensate.

findings.headline: Commercial income pressures mounting: £600k cumulative loss from pavements shopping centre
findings.detail: The council faces a £300k combined pressure from reduced income at Pavements shopping centre and other commercial property in 2026/27 (£100k further pressure in 2027/28). This is cumulative with previous income reductions already built into the 2025/26 budget, bringing the overall reduction to £600k. The council notes this "will continue to be monitored and considered as part of future budget planning."
findings.matters: A key commercial asset (Pavements shopping centre) is underperforming, generating cumulative £600k income loss. Commercial property income is volatile and difficult to recover, putting future service funding at risk.
findings.figures: 2026/27 pressure £200k (pavements) plus £100k (shopping centre); cumulative reduction £600k; further 2027/28 pressure £100k
findings.quote: Pavements Shopping Centre/Commercial property income – combined £300k has been included in the MTFP presenting previous profile and new pressure. This is above and beyond previous income reductions included in the 2025/26 budget that bring the overall reduction to £600k.

findings.headline: Recruitment and retention challenges driving unexpected agency and interim cost pressures
findings.detail: Across the council, ongoing recruitment difficulties (particularly technical and professional roles) mean vacancy savings are being offset by agency and interim staff costs. Legal Services alone is spending £381k on interim appointments to cover vacancies pending permanent recruitment, with a net overspend of £115k. The council acknowledges this is consistent across the public sector but notes it means cost assumptions are becoming less robust.
findings.matters: What was budgeted as savings (vacancies) is materializing as costs (agency premiums). This suggests either service delivery risk (unfilled posts) or cost volatility (agency spend). The CFO notes this makes estimates "inevitably less robust than we would like them to be."
findings.figures: Legal Services interim costs £381k; net Legal Services overspend £115k; overall service budget variance £146k favourable (after offsetting savings)
findings.quote: Whilst savings from vacant posts remain likely, due to ongoing recruitment and retention challenges, these are increasingly offset by additional costs from agency and interim resources.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account working balance projected to fall below statutory minimum
findings.detail: The HRA working balance is projected to fall to £2.7m in 2026/27, below the statutory minimum of £3.7m. This is driven by ongoing financial pressures including rising maintenance costs, voids, disrepair claims, and capital investment. While the council expects improvement in later years and does not expect revenue contributions to capital until 2030/31, the 2026/27 shortfall represents a material statutory risk.
findings.matters: A statutory reserve falling below minimum indicates housing finances under stress. The delay until 2030/31 before revenues can support capital investment limits the council's ability to refresh ageing housing stock.
findings.figures: 2026/27 projected HRA working balance £2.7m; statutory minimum £3.7m; no revenue to capital contribution until 2030/31
findings.quote: The MTPF shows that for 2026/27 the working balance is projected to fall to £2.7m, which would be below the minimum working balance of £3.7m.

findings.headline: Government settlement methodology change creates cumulative £1.3m uncompensated funding loss beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: MHCLG made late changes (announced 9 February 2026, after provisional settlement) to how pooling gains are rolled into the settlement, shifting funds from shire districts to counties. Chesterfield receives a one-off £0.826m Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27 to offset the change, but this grant does not recur. Cumulative uncompensated reductions are £0.714m in 2027/28 and £0.616m in 2028/29—neither addressed in the MTFP.
findings.matters: The council is hit by a structural loss of government funding that it cannot control or plan for. The timing and design of the settlement change (late notice, methodology shift benefiting counties over districts) suggests further regulatory/funding risk.
findings.figures: One-off Adjustment Support Grant £0.826m in 2026/27; uncompensated reductions £0.714m (2027/28) and £0.616m (2028/29)
findings.quote: MHCLG belatedly decided to change the methodology used to roll-in previous pooling gains into the assumed 2025/26 business rates income. This change broadly shifts the pooling gains away from shire districts to shire counties.

findings.headline: Unresolved budget gaps of £2.8m (2027/28) and £3.4m (2028/29) with reserves deemed unsustainable solution
findings.detail: Whilst the 2026/27 budget is balanced (using £273k reserve draw), the medium-term plan shows cumulative gaps of £2.842m in 2027/28 and £3.360m in 2028/29. The CFO explicitly states reserves cannot sustainably fund this scale of gap. The council notes it has not balanced the MTFP and must start the 2027/28 budget process early to identify savings options. No major funding improvements are expected, and further council tax increases are already assumed at maximum.
findings.matters: A lender is looking at a council that has deferred hard choices by using reserves, faces deteriorating position, and has limited options: no scope for extra government funding, income targets already realistic, and maximum council tax rises already assumed.
findings.figures: 2026/27 balance requires £273k Budget Risk reserve use; 2027/28 gap £2.842m; 2028/29 gap £3.360m
findings.quote: Continuing to use reserves is not sustainable so the 2027/28 budget process will need to start early in the next financial year so as to allow early focus and maximum time for the development and delivery of further budget savings options.

findings.headline: Careline service running structural deficit with reserve depletion in sight
findings.detail: The Careline (aged care alarm service) is operating below cost-neutral customer levels and cannot forecast break-even. Weekly charges would need to rise to £28 (vs £14.50 currently charged) to reach cost neutrality. The £300k Careline reserve established in 2024/25 will be fully depleted by 2026/27. A further review including public consultation is underway to consider closure, redesign, or collaboration, with up to £400k capital receipts flexibility set aside for transformation.
findings.matters: A material service (operating at £1.2m income target) is loss-making and dependent on reserves. The council has signalled it may close or materially redesign the service, with consultation to follow.
findings.figures: Current weekly charge £14.50, cost-neutral charge £28; annual income target £1.2m; reserve depletion by 2026/27; £300k Careline reserve; £400k capital receipts flexibility held for transformation
findings.quote: At the end of period 9 the actual customer numbers are below target and the service is not currently able to forecast a year-end break-even position. Revised projections now estimate that the weekly charge necessary to achieve cost neutrality has risen to £28.

findings.headline: Decent Homes compliance not yet at 100 per cent; council is currently at 99.5 per cent with properties still affected by damp and mould
findings.detail: As of December 2025, 99.5% of housing stock meets the Decent Homes Standard. The council states that delivery of the programme will lead to 100% compliance and 'a considerable reduction in the number of properties affected by damp and mould'. This indicates active compliance gaps despite legal duties under Awaab's Law.
findings.matters: A lender must know whether the council has any breach of statutory duties (Awaab's Law, Housing Act 2004, Homes Fitness for Human Habitation Act) or regulatory breaches that could trigger intervention or enforcement action by the Regulator of Social Housing.
findings.figures: 99.5% current compliance; target 100%; gap of 0.5% of stock still not meeting standard as of December 2025
findings.quote: Currently, 99.5% of the housing stock meets the Decent Homes Standard (as of December 2025), and delivery of the programme will lead to 100% compliance with the standard, as well as a considerable reduction in the number of properties affected by damp and mould.

findings.headline: Mastin Moor new build scheme requires external grant funding because remediation costs are exceptionally high
findings.detail: An 18-home new build scheme at Mastin Moor, commenced September 2025, is dependent on grant funding from the East Midlands Combined County Authority because 'extensive land remediation work' is required. The council cannot fund this from its own resources alone.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know which schemes depend on grant funding and whether they proceed if that funding is withdrawn or delayed. Remediation cost escalation is also a warning sign.
findings.figures: 18 new council homes; grant funding from East Midlands Combined County Authority; grant work concluding during 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the high cost of the scheme resulting from extensive land remediation work, a bid for grant funding has been approved by the East Midlands Combined County Authority.

findings.headline: Brocklehurst Court decarbonisation project delayed by power supply constraints from Distribution Network Operator
findings.detail: A flagship decarbonisation scheme at Brocklehurst Court independent living scheme, involving air source heat pumps and solar panels, has been delayed due to Distribution Network Operator power supply issues. The project was originally expected to complete earlier but is now due to complete in Summer 2026.
findings.matters: Project delays on council capital schemes can signal delivery risk and may indicate constraints (e.g. infrastructure availability) that affect other schemes. This one is dependent on external parties.
findings.figures: 1 of 6 independent living schemes; completion now Summer 2026
findings.quote: Unfortunately, the Brocklehurst Court project has been delayed due to Distribution Network Operator issues with power supply and is now due to complete in Summer 2026.

findings.headline: HRA Business Plan sustainability at risk if borrowing is not reduced and redirected to new homes only
findings.detail: The risk register flags this as high impact and high likelihood. The council faces a 'challenging financial position of the Housing Revenue Account' and cannot contribute to the capital programme from revenue until 2029/30. The Business Plan itself is sensitive to assumptions around rent rises, inflation, interest rates, voids and right-to-buy sales, with the council noting small changes 'can, particularly over time, have a significant effect on the sustainability of the Plan'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the HRA's debt servicing assumptions hold under stress, whether revenue pressure could force cuts, and whether the council has modelled the risk from interest rate movements.
findings.figures: 2026/27 programme £33.982m; no revenue contribution until 2029/30; borrowing planned from 2027/28 (£6.985m) onwards.
findings.quote: Given the challenging financial position of the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) a direct revenue financing contribution towards the Programme is not currently feasible until 2029/2030.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: Multiple new housing regulations require capital investment with no funding identified until 2029-30
findings.detail: Awaab's Law (Phase 1 from October 2025), reformed Decent Homes Standard (from 2035), Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (2030 and 2039 deadlines), and new Social Housing Regulation require capital investment. The council notes these will increase capital requirements but does not identify funding sources until 2029-30 when a £5.097m revenue contribution is planned.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance is non-negotiable. Underfunding compliance causes service failure, audit criticism, and potential enforcement action. Deferring funding to 2029-30 compresses response time and may force emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Revenue contribution to capital: £0 for 2026-27, 2027-28, 2028-29; £5.097m in 2029-30
findings.quote: These changes are likely to increase capital investment requirements for compliance and future maintenance programmes.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: Voluntary debt repayment paused and reintroduced at lower level, signalling cash pressure
findings.detail: The council's planned £1.5m annual voluntary debt repayment was suspended and budget reallocated to pay protection for trades staff. When reintroduced for 2026-27, it is reduced to £500k, increasing to £750k in 2027-28 before returning to normal. This reflects that the HRA cannot afford the originally planned debt service.
findings.matters: Deferring voluntary debt repayment indicates the council prioritised employee obligations (pay protection) over balance-sheet strength. At high debt levels, reduced repayment capacity limits deleveraging and extends debt duration.
findings.figures: Voluntary repayment suspended in 2025-26; reintroduced at £500k (2026-27), £750k (2027-28), returning to standard level thereafter vs original £1.5m
findings.quote: the budget for 2025/26 assumed a sum of £1.5m for the voluntary repayment of debt. This was paused for a further 12 months and the budget repurposed to cover the one-off costs of pay protection for trades staff.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: Current year 2025-26 deficit exceeded budget by £1m, signalling forecast accuracy issues
findings.detail: The 2025-26 deficit forecast worsened from £2.965m (February estimate) to £3.981m, a variance of £1.016m. Main drivers are higher void rates (£361k), repairs overspend (£562k), and one-off pay protection costs (£1.392m). This tracking worse than expected creates confidence questions for future years' forecasts.
findings.matters: Large in-year forecast variance indicates either weak budget setting or emerging problems the council did not anticipate. This compounds concerns about reliance on future savings and reducing void rates.
findings.figures: 2025-26 deficit variance: £1.016m worse than latest estimate; repairs overspend £562k; pay protection one-off £1.392m; void-related losses £361k + £86k
findings.quote: The deficit for 2025/26 is forecast to be £3.981m (as at period 8), which is a variance of £1.016m against the latest estimate.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: Government rent policy removed £61m of projected income over 30-year plan period
findings.detail: The 2023-24 government-mandated 7% rent cap (below inflation) removed £1.5m annual income in perpetuity. When combined with four-year rent reductions between 2016-2020, the cumulative income loss over the 30-year business plan is £61m. The council can only partially recover through 2.5% annual increases (CPI+1%) and new rent convergence policy.
findings.matters: Structural income loss of this magnitude is permanent and unrecoverable. It fundamentally constrains the HRA's ability to invest and maintain stock to standards, forcing either higher borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: £1.5m annual income loss from 2023-24 rent cap; £61m loss over business plan period; current rent increase limited to 4.8% for 2026-27
findings.quote: The mandated rent cap of 7% in 2023/24 (which was 4.1% less than inflation), had the cumulative impact of removing £1.5m of annual income (after voids) in perpetuity, with an estimated loss over the business plan period in terms of income of £61m.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: HRA debt projected to peak at £153m, near ceiling limits
findings.detail: The 30-year business plan shows new borrowing required through year 5 with total debt peaking at £153m. While stated to remain below the council's optional debt cap, this is only slightly below the original £156m government-imposed ceiling that was removed in 2018. The council relies on government policy not imposing new caps.
findings.matters: High debt levels relative to income constrain financial flexibility. The proximity to historical ceilings and reliance on future government policy creates refinancing risk if sentiment changes, particularly given the regulatory focus on local authority finances.
findings.figures: Debt peak of £153m projected; compares to original £156m debt ceiling; interest costs rising from £4.578m in 2026-27 to £5.450m by 2029-30
findings.quote: The business plan assumes that new borrowing will be required up to year 5, with total debt peaking at £153m. This level of borrowing remains below the Council's optional debt cap, ensuring that the HRA stays within its prudential limits.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: Void properties worse than expected, creating unbudgeted costs in current and next year
findings.detail: Actual void rate for 2025-26 reached 3.85%, against original budget assumption of 2.5%. This creates £361k additional rent loss and £186k in additional council tax costs (£100k). The budget for 2026-27 assumes voids will reduce to 3.5%, with additional costs of £465k lost rental income and £100k council tax.
findings.matters: Voids directly reduce income and increase costs. Persistent underperformance signals either declining demand, property condition issues, or management problems, any of which affects the sustainability of the housing business model.
findings.figures: Actual void rate 3.85% vs 2.5% budgeted; rent loss £361k in 2025-26; 2026-27 additional void costs £465k rent loss + £100k council tax
findings.quote: The actual void rate for 2025/26 is approximately 3.85%, resulting in further rent loss. There will however be additional costs associated with the current levels of void properties in 2026/27 of an additional £465k in lost rental income and £100k in additional council tax payments.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Budget Report 2026-27 and MTFP
findings.headline: HRA working balance projected to fall below minimum safe level in 2026-27
findings.detail: The council's HRA working balance is forecast to drop to £2.7m in 2026-27, below the required minimum of £3.7m. The council identifies this as arising from ongoing pressures including rising maintenance costs, voids, disrepair claims, and capital investment plans.
findings.matters: A local authority housing account falling below prudent minimum reserves signals financial stress and constrains the council's ability to absorb shocks or fund capital investment without borrowing.
findings.figures: £2.7m projected balance against £3.7m minimum; minimum working balance stated as £3.7m (increased annually by inflation)
findings.quote: The MTPF shows that for 2026/27 the working balance is projected to fall to £2.7m, which is below the minimum working balance of £3.7m. This projected situation has arisen as a result of ongoing financial pressures, particularly in relation to rising maintenance costs, voids, disrepair claims, and capital investment plans.

news_drafts.headline: MTFP forecasts £2.842m funding gap in 2027/28, rising to £3.360m in 2028/29
news_drafts.lead: The council faces significant structural funding gaps ahead that it plans to cover with reserve draws rather than sustainable savings. The underspend is being treated as a tool to manage MTFP gaps, not strengthen the balance sheet.

news_drafts.headline: £572k of housing repairs shifted from capital to revenue, indicating capital maintenance underfunding
news_drafts.lead: Shifting maintenance from capital to revenue increases annual cost pressures on rents and indicates the HRA may be underfunding capital maintenance, with reactive maintenance bleeding into revenue.

news_drafts.headline: HRA working balance at £3.117m is below the prudent minimum of £3.7m with ongoing void rate stress
news_drafts.lead: Housing finance is operating with reserves below the prudent minimum, and actual rental income is under pressure from void rates significantly above the long-term business plan assumption. This constrains HRA financial flexibility.
